title: After 1997, southern Australian streams drained 11% faster at equal flow, and lower pre-storm flow explained half of the smaller storm runoff (353 CAMELS-AUS catchments, 1951-2021)
abstract: Question: southern Australian runoff fell below its 1951-1996 rainfall-runoff relation from 1997 and stayed low to 2021. Is this a smaller storm response at equal catchment wetness, or only lower storage before storms? Did streams drain faster at equal flow? Approach: we used daily CAMELS-AUS v2.03 data for 353 southern and 156 northern (control) catchments and 335,042 southern storm events. A per-catchment Poisson regression fitted on 1951-1996 events gave the expected event runoff; we added storm rain and season, antecedent rain, and the observed pre-event flow step by step. On rain-free days, we compared the rate of flow decrease with the 1951-1996 rate in the same flow bin. Intervals are cluster-bootstrap intervals; a 1981-1996 break gives the placebo value. Results: in 1997-2021, southern storm runoff was 36% below expectation at equal storm rain and season (log ratio -0.44, 95% CI -0.57 to -0.32; placebo -0.09; north -0.07). Pre-event flow was 42% lower. With pre-event flow in the model, the deficit was -0.19 (-0.28 to -0.11); lower pre-storm wetness explained 56% (48-68%) of the deficit. The remaining deficit at equal pre-event flow was -0.12 (-0.20 to -0.04) relative to the placebo with AGCD rain and -0.03 (-0.11 to +0.07) with SILO rain. Southern recessions were 11% faster at equal flow (+0.10 log units, +0.08 to +0.13; placebo -0.03), in 1997-2009 and 2010-2021, in the cool and warm seasons and at all flow levels; northern recessions were slower (-0.15). Across southern catchments, faster drainage went with lower pre-event flow (rho -0.43) and a larger annual deficit (rho -0.34), but not with the rain change (rho -0.09). Conclusion: after 1997, southern catchments lost water faster from the store that feeds streams, and the lower pre-storm wetness explains about half of the smaller storm runoff. This agrees better with more loss from that store (for example to a falling water table) than with less recharge alone. Limitations: the main estimators were added after the planned estimators showed a bias; no groundwater, water-use or vegetation data; the physical process is not identified.

citations.reason: Starting point: the southern Australian post-1997 deficit that does not scale with the rain deficit. Our recession change does not depend on the rain change.
Baseflow and quickflow both fell; we show a mechanism that lowers both.
Baseflow fell more than an effective-rain loss predicts; faster drainage of the stream-connected store agrees with this.
Fixed gauge networks confirm the shift; our recession test does not use rain amounts.
Era-dependent post-drought deficit; the eastern US shift was not tested here.
Daily rain summaries did not remove the deficit; our event analysis conditions on storm rain directly.
